transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-23
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), David Ortiz (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (CTO - Aquila), Elena Ruiz (SRE Lead - Aquila), Tom Walker (Infra - Aquila)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
Customer interested in making sure that if a region degrades we can fail traffic without causing cascading availability issues; they want deterministic rollback policy and visibility into token/lifecycle accounting across fallback variants.

00:00:12 Maya (Redwood AE): Hey all, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account, with me is David, our systems engineer who does the heavy lifting on routing and private deployments. How are you folks doing?
00:00:22 Samir (CTO - Aquila): Good, Maya. Thanks. We're trying to get a concise plan for how to handle a regional slowdown for our customer-facing summarization service. The big ask: when a region gets degraded, what's the traffic steering strategy and how do we roll back?
00:00:40 David (Redwood SE): Great question. We typically recommend a three-tier approach: 1) local retry and KV-cache priming, 2) regional steering to healthy region replicas, and 3) fallback to lower-cost / lower-capacity model variants if capacity is constrained. But each step has SLO tradeoffs.
00:01:05 Elena (SRE - Aquila): When you say "lower-capacity model variants" — like a quantized 4-bit variant? Does that change semantics? We can't have hallucinations spike in production.
00:01:18 David (Redwood SE): Right, quantized variants can introduce small quality deltas. We have evaluation hooks and can tie rollout policies to prompt set regressions. For critical endpoints we'd do canary traffic to the quantized model, and only route after passing QA thresholds.
00:01:40 Tom (Infra - Aquila): Our legal/security team will push back on any cross-region data transfer for some customers — we have EU residency requirements. How does Redwood handle data residency when you steer to another region?
00:01:56 Maya (Redwood AE): Good point — that's where Dedicated or Private usually comes in. For Hosted, we can restrict routing to regions within the acceptable geography, and we provide audit logs + configurable retention. For strict residency you can use Private (VPC) or on-prem. We'll share the notes on how routing policies respect region-level residency tags.
00:02:20 Speaker 2: (unidentified) Also curious on KMS integration — we need customer-managed keys.
00:02:27 David (Redwood SE): We support KMS/HSM integration for Private deployments; Hosted also supports envelope encryption with bring-your-own-key (BYOK) in some regions. We'll put the exact flow in the security doc.
00:02:40 Elena (SRE): Cool. Can you walk us through a concrete rollback flow? Like if latency p95 in region us-west spikes above 900ms for 5m what happens?
00:02:52 David (Redwood SE): Sure. Example operator flow:
- Detection: observability triggers when p95>900ms for >3 minutes.
- Automated mitigation: route a percentage of traffic (start 10-20%) to alternate region (us-east), keep remainder with circuit-breaker style backoff to us-west.
- Prime caches in target region with prefix caching to avoid cold-start tails.
- If success metrics (latency and error %) improve, ramp to 50% then full failover.
- If errors increase or quality regressions are detected, automatic rollback to previous model and region.

00:03:32 Samir (CTO): And who manages the rollback orchestration? Is that Redwood's control plane or our ops?
00:03:39 Maya (Redwood AE): You can choose. For Dedicated and Hosted we provide automated routing policies managed by Redwood, with webhook hooks into your incident system. For Private, you have the control plane and can run the same routing plugin internally. Most customers want Redwood to own initial rollback, but ops retains the final kill switch.

00:04:02 Elena (SRE): In practice, how fast is the cutover? We're concerned about session stickiness and user experience for chat flows.
00:04:12 David (Redwood SE): With prefix cache priming and stateful KV cache transfer we aim for sub-500ms per-request added latency during gradual shift; full convergence depends on session affinity TTLs — typical rolling window is 30–90s for chat sessions if you keep sticky keys. We can also do token-level binding to avoid breaking conversation context.

00:04:40 Tom (Infra): If we do a cross-region failover, does that double our cost (e.g., CPU/GPU charge in both regions during ramp)?
00:04:48 Maya (Redwood AE): There's transient duplicate cost while both pools run. We can model that in the cost estimate — the failover matrix we'll send includes an expected peak-cost delta and suggestion for reserved burst capacity to avoid two full-size pools.

00:05:12 Samir: We're evaluating three deployment options: Hosted, Dedicated, Private. The business wants predictable latency and cost. Can you outline the reliability differences?
00:05:26 David: High-level: Hosted gives fastest time-to-value and Redwood-managed SLOs, Dedicated gives reserved capacity + stronger isolation and predictable throughput (good for 24/7 latency targets), Private gives full control for residency and compliance but requires your ops to manage switchover. We can provide SLA tiers: 99.9% vs 99.95% depending on reserved capacity and region redundancy.

00:05:55 Elena: Is there a written SLA for individual endpoint latency thresholds or just availability?
00:06:01 Maya: Our contractual SLAs are availability-focused, but we provide latency SLOs in our performance profiles and recommend Dual-region deployment for tighter p95 SLAs. We can include latency SLOs as part of an enterprise addendum.

00:06:20 Samir: What about partial degradation — say storage backend to the model store has a hiccup; do requests queue and cause cascading backpressure?
00:06:31 David: Redwood runtime uses continuous batching and request shedding with priority tiers. Non-critical background evals will be dropped first; customer-facing inference has higher priority. Also KV cache and prefix caching reduce pressure on model store. We'll show an example runbook for shedding thresholds.

00:06:58 Elena: I want to see circuit-breaker thresholds. Our oncall needs exact numbers to set PagerDuty rules.
00:07:05 David: We'll include suggested thresholds (p95 > 800ms or error rate > 1% triggers 10% traffic reroute). Those are starting points; they should be tuned per workload.

00:07:25 Tom: For Private deployment, does Redwood still push runtime updates or do we have to pull?
00:07:32 Maya: For Private (VPC or on-prem), you control upgrades. We provide release notes, migration tools, and a managed option where Redwood can perform updates under a schedule. We also support air-gapped installs for regulated customers.

00:07:48 Speaker 1 (unidentified): Do you have examples of customers who ran a live rollback?
00:07:54 Maya: Yes—we have a case study (redacted) where a retail customer rolled back after a quantized model introduced a class of hallucinations. We automated canary rollback after quality regressions flagged by their eval suite. We'll share a sanitized runbook.

00:08:10 Samir: We need to simulate region flapping. Can you help with chaos tests?
00:08:15 David: Absolutely. We run synthetic traffic and chaos injection tests as part of initial pilots. For Dedicated customers we can run joint exercises and handoff docs for your SREs.

00:08:30 Elena: We're also concerned about observability — we need token-level tracing, model version, and per-route latency.
00:08:38 David: Redwood Console exposes per-route/model dashboards, trace IDs, token breakdown, and KV cache hit rates. You can export traces to your existing tracing backend.

00:08:50 Tom: If we do a failover, do we lose model KV cache and need a cold start?
00:08:57 David: There's some cold-start risk but we mitigate via prefix priming. For very large contexts we recommend warm replicas in standby or a hot standby model with a smaller memory footprint to avoid long cold tails.

00:09:15 Samir: About routing granularity: can we route by customer ID, tenant, or route path?
00:09:23 Maya: Yes, routing policies can be route-level or token/tenant-level. You can configure policies so specific enterprise tenants never cross region boundaries.

00:09:40 Elena: For audit compliance, we need immutable logs for any routing decision.
00:09:46 David: We provide audit logs with routing decisions, timestamps, and the associated trace IDs. For Dedicated/Private you can increase retention. We'll send log retention options in the doc package.

00:10:05 Samir: Let's talk numbers — our optimistic p95 target is 200ms, p99 under 600ms. Can Redwood hit that from EU region with our current traffic profile?
00:10:16 David: Depends on model size and request length. For a 13B model quantized to int8 and good batching we can approach p95 200–300ms in a colocated region. We'll need your token distribution and average prompt length. The benchmark run we propose will simulate your exact prompts.

00:10:42 Tom: Regarding cross-region bandwidth, we have limits on egress costs. If we steer 30% traffic to us-east from eu-west, that increases egress and may violate cost caps.
00:10:51 Maya: We'll include per-scenario egress estimates. Also we can bias steering to a nearer fallover region (e.g., eu-central) to minimize egress.

00:11:05 Elena: Is there a way to do graceful degradation of model outputs rather than just swapping models? For example, reduce max tokens or disable non-essential features.
00:11:16 David: Yes, we recommend feature flags for quality-cost tradeoffs: lowering max_tokens, turning off generation sampling features, or switching to a cheaper reranker for non-critical paths. Redwood Optimize can suggest profiles.

00:11:30 Samir: For the benchmarking window, we'd like to run sustained 10k concurrent users for 30 minutes. Can Redwood simulate that against Hosted?
00:11:39 David: Yes, we can provision a scheduling window and isolate load to avoid noisy neighbor effects. For Hosted we may need to bump to dedicated test capacity depending on model size.

00:11:52 Maya: Quick note on pricing — Dedicated has a reserved/month commitment; Hosted is usage-based and may spike during failover events. We'll model both.

00:12:02 Tom: On the security front, do you support SAML SSO and RBAC for team access?
00:12:08 Maya: Yes, SAML/SSO and fine-grained RBAC are supported. For Dedicated we offer enforced IP allowlists and VPC peering.

00:12:20 Elena: How about incident notification integration? We need automatic webhook to our incident system to trigger runbooks.
00:12:26 David: Redwood supports webhooks and can integrate with PagerDuty/Splunk/Slack. We can push alerts when routing policy engages or when model quality drops.

00:12:40 Samir: Are there any gotchas we should be aware of when using optimistic auto-fallbacks?
00:12:47 David: Two main gotchas: 1) quality drift with different quantization or model families — you should have regression tests and canary thresholds; 2) double-cost during ramp — plan for transient capacity. Also network egress and data residency constraints can limit your available fallback regions.

00:13:05 Maya: I'll pause and see if there are any obvious PLs and timelines. Samir, what is your desired timeline for an initial pilot?
00:13:12 Samir: We want a pilot in the next 3 weeks and a production rollout by end of Q4 if the pilot looks good. Security review is on the critical path.
00:13:23 Maya: Ok — we can do a pilot window week of 2027-08-30. We'll be sending the SOC2 + network diagrams this week.

00:13:30 Elena: One more question about replication lag — how do you keep model parameters and custom embeddings in sync across regions when we have continuous updates?
00:13:40 David: We use eventual-consistent push; embeddings and feature stores are best synchronized via your canonical store (S3/DB). For model parameters we version the model and deploy atomically. For customer-specific embeddings, Redwood supports syncing via scheduled jobs or a near-realtime replication pipeline depending on your tolerance.

00:13:58 Tom: Is there a recommended rollout policy for model changes to minimize incident risk?
00:14:05 David: Canary by tenant coupled with automated quality checks. Start with 1% of traffic for a day, measure key metrics and regression evals, then ramp 10%/hour with automatic rollback if your eval suite fails.

00:14:25 Speaker 3 (unidentified): How do you handle upstream vendor outages — e.g., underlying cloud region OOM or AZ down?
00:14:32 Maya: Our multi-region routing is designed to fail over at the Redwood control plane level; if a cloud AZ dies we shift to other AZs or regions per policy. For Dedicated we have reserved cross-AZ pools. For Private, you need to provision standby capacity.

00:14:48 Samir: Would you be able to provide a concrete runbook example where the system automatically reroutes and then rolls back after quality check failure?
00:14:56 David: Yes, we'll attach a sanitized runbook with step-by-step triggers and exact thresholds, and an example of a rollback webhook payload you can integrate with.

00:15:10 Elena: Let's talk about metrics. Which ones should we instrument in our dashboards?
00:15:16 David: p50/p95/p99 latency, error % (5xx), token throughput, KV cache hit rate, model version distribution, and quality regression metric (BLEU/ROUGE or custom classifier for hallucinations).

00:15:34 Maya: Anything else from the team?
00:15:38 Tom: Just to confirm — after the benchmark we get a results packet with cost modelling, suggested routing policy, and recommended Dedicated capacity?
00:15:46 Maya: Correct. We'll produce a Failover Matrix PDF with cost impacts and a recommended Dedicated sizing if you want a reserved lane.

00:16:00 Samir: Ok good. I want to call out one enterprise requirement: any fallback to US regions must be opt-in for EU customers; otherwise we must keep EU only.
00:16:11 David: We can set tenant-level region constraints so EU customers never leave EU regions. That will be documented.

00:16:20 Elena: For the pilot, please include a small chaos test we run with you in a session so we can exercise the rollback.
00:16:27 Maya: We'll schedule a co-run.

00:35:07 David: It emits a structured event with trace IDs, affected model/version, routing delta, and the evaluation verdict. It also posts to the webhook you configure.

00:37:29 Maya: Yes typically contractual latency guarantees require reserved capacity and redundancy. We'll outline what levels require which commitments.
